title: Safe Subscript Extension
hints: Subscripts can have argument labels, and you can add them in an extension.
In `extension Collection`, return `self[index]` only if `indices.contains(index)`, else `nil`.
`subscript(safe index: Index) -> Element? { indices.contains(index) ? self[index] : nil }` and `indices.map { items[safe: $0] }`.
jsBridge: JS returns `undefined` for out-of-range reads and never crashes. Swift traps, deliberately. A `subscript(safe:)` extension restores the optional behaviour where you want it, and extensions on `Collection` apply to arrays, strings and slices at once.

compass.q: Is Swift's crash-on-out-of-bounds better than JS's silent `undefined`? Argue both sides for an app with millions of users.
Java throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException`, which you can catch. Swift's trap can't be caught. Why did Swift choose a non-recoverable failure?
Why must the check be `indices.contains(i)`, not `i < count`? Think of `ArraySlice` and `String`.
`items[safe: indexPath.row]` in table-view code is common. Is it hiding a real bug (a data-source mismatch) that you should fix instead?
